overview: Corythosaurus casuarius ("helmeted lizard") was a large crested hadrosaur from the Campanian of Alberta (~77–75 Ma), reaching about nine metres and distinguished by a tall, thin helmet-like hollow crest on the skull. The crest contained looping nasal passages that may have allowed deep, resonant calls — the most well-supported hypothesis for hollow hadrosaur crests generally.

Exceptional preservation of Corythosaurus skin impressions reveals a complex mosaic of large polygonal scales and smaller tubercles. The crest shape changed through ontogeny: juveniles had small rounded crests, young adults showed intermediate forms and large adults had the full helmet. This ontogenetic change helps distinguish Corythosaurus from the closely related Lambeosaurus.

fossilSites.name: Dinosaur Park Formation
fossilSites.note: Campanian coastal plain deposits with abundant Corythosaurus material including mummified specimens with skin impressions.

articles.title: Discovery
articles.body: Described by Barnum Brown in 1914 from Dinosaur Park Formation material. Brown collected several Corythosaurus specimens including a "mummy" with skin impressions. The crest — formed by the nasal and frontal bones — immediately distinguished it from flat-headed hadrosaurs. Juvenile skulls show progressive crest development that helped establish ontogenetic series for the species.

articles.title: Crest function
articles.body: The hollow crest of Corythosaurus contained elaborately looping nasal passages. When air was pushed through these passages, they would produce low-frequency resonant sounds specific to each crest shape — allowing individual species recognition, mate attraction and herd communication. Modern analogues include the resonating chambers of howler monkeys and some hornbills.

articles.title: Skin and appearance
articles.body: Multiple Corythosaurus specimens preserve skin impressions across the neck, body and tail. The skin shows a pebbly texture with larger tubercles forming a mosaic. No direct colour evidence is preserved, but countershading (darker back, lighter belly) is commonly assumed for camouflage. The crest was probably brightly coloured and used in display, as in modern cassowaries.

record.description: Corythosaurus casuarius was a helmet-crested lambeosaurine hadrosaurid from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta. Many skulls and skeletons across growth stages, including skin impressions, document its anatomy and the dramatic ontogenetic growth of its hollow crest.
facts: The internal nasal passages of the crest are preserved and could affect sound resonance, but no specific call can be reconstructed as fact.
Many historical Corythosaurus species are now interpreted as growth or individual variation within C. casuarius.

presentation.heroLead: A helmet-crested duck-billed dinosaur from Alberta, known from complete skeletons with skin impressions and from a growth series that shows its hollow crest inflating with age.

animalParagraphs: Corythosaurus was a large duck-billed dinosaur of the lambeosaurine group that lived along the river plains of what is now southern Alberta in the late Campanian. Adults were about eight to nine metres long and could walk on either two or four legs, with a deep tail stiffened by ossified tendons.

Its most striking feature was a tall, rounded bony crest that gave the animal its name, meaning "helmet lizard". The crest was hollow and housed looping nasal passages; because the airway is preserved inside the bone, its shape is known directly, although what sounds it may have produced is a matter of modelling rather than observation.

Skulls of many sizes show that juveniles had only a low bump where the adult crest would later rise. Several species named from Alberta in the early twentieth century are now regarded as growth stages or individual variants of Corythosaurus casuarius, although a second, stratigraphically higher species, C. intermedius, is still recognised by some workers.
animalHighlights: A tall, hollow, helmet-shaped crest containing the nasal passages, which grew dramatically between juvenile and adult stages.
Skin impressions preserved on the holotype and a second skeleton show a covering of small, non-overlapping scales.
One of the most completely known hadrosaurids, with near-complete articulated skeletons collected from the Dinosaur Park Formation.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Supported by beak and dental batteries
lifeCards.reason: A broad, toothless beak and dental batteries of hundreds of closely packed teeth with grinding wear are directly preserved. Reported gut contents from an early specimen are of uncertain reliability.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Complete fore- and hindlimbs with hoof-like hand and foot bones fit a hadrosaurid that shifted between two- and four-legged walking. Speeds are modelled, not observed.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Near-complete articulated adults allow length to be measured directly; body mass is still an estimate.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Skin impressions record scale size and pattern over parts of the body, but colour, any soft crest extensions and other integument are inferred.

locality.note: The holotype was collected by Barnum Brown in 1912 from the Belly River beds, now the Dinosaur Park Formation. Corythosaurus material is largely confined to the lower part of the formation.

presentation.classificationSummary: Corythosaurus is a lambeosaurine hadrosaurid, part of the hollow-crested duck-billed dinosaurs. It is consistently grouped with Hypacrosaurus and Lambeosaurus among the helmet-crested lambeosaurines.

related.reason: Compare with the hatchet-crested lambeosaurine that occurs slightly higher in the same formation.
Compare with a closely related helmet-crested lambeosaurine known from nests and embryos.
Compare with a tube-crested lambeosaurine whose crest housed a much longer airway.

questions.title: What did the crest do?
questions.copy: The looping nasal passages could have resonated during calls and the crest probably served in visual display, but neither function can be confirmed directly, and no specific call can be reconstructed as fact.

questions.title: How many species are valid?
questions.copy: Growth-stage studies collapsed several early names into C. casuarius. Whether C. intermedius is a distinct, younger species or variation within one lineage is still discussed.

questions.title: What was lost at sea?
questions.copy: Two Corythosaurus skeletons collected by the Sternbergs were lost in 1916 when the ship carrying them to Britain was sunk, so part of the early material survives only in field records.

review.ageReviewNote: Diagnostic C. casuarius material is late Campanian in the Dinosaur Park Formation.

specimens.name: Holotype
specimens.institution: American Museum of Natural History, New York
specimens.note: A nearly complete articulated skeleton with skin impressions, collected by Barnum Brown in 1912 from the Red Deer River and described in 1914.

specimens.name: Referred skeleton
specimens.institution: American Museum of Natural History, New York
specimens.note: A second near-complete skeleton with extensive skin impressions, described by Brown in 1916 and displayed in New York.

panel.headline: Complete skeletons, skin impressions and a growth series of crested skulls.
panel.standfirst: Corythosaurus has one of the best fossil records of any hadrosaurid. The holotype and a second New York skeleton are nearly complete and articulated with skin, and many further skulls and skeletons from the Dinosaur Park Formation span juvenile to adult growth stages.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every region of the skeleton is known from multiple articulated individuals, with skin impressions and a juvenile-to-adult skull series.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Complete skulls with crests and dental batteries, full vertebral series with ossified tendons, both girdles, all four limbs with hands and feet, and impressions of scaly skin over the flank, limbs and tail in at least two individuals.
knownRemains.note: The main gaps are not skeletal: the keratin beak, any soft-tissue crest extension, colour and the acoustic behaviour of the living animal are not preserved.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Many complete skulls with hollow crests and internal nasal passages, beaks, dental batteries and braincases, from small juveniles to large adults.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Complete cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series with ribs, chevrons and the lattice of ossified tendons along the back and tail.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Complete pectoral and pelvic girdles, forelimbs with hooved hands and hindlimbs with feet, articulated in several skeletons.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Skin impressions with small polygonal scales on the holotype and AMNH 5338; possible gut contents were reported from early material but are not securely attributed.

specimenCards.title: AMNH 5240 · holotype
specimenCards.description: A nearly complete articulated skeleton with skin impressions, found by Barnum Brown in 1912 in the Red Deer River badlands and described by him in 1914. It lacks only parts of the forelimbs and tail tip.
specimenCards.meta: Red Deer River · Dinosaur Park Formation · American Museum of Natural History

specimenCards.title: AMNH 5338 · referred skeleton
specimenCards.description: A second near-complete skeleton described by Brown in 1916 with extensive skin impressions, which formed the basis of his reconstruction of the animal's musculature and epidermis.
specimenCards.meta: Red Deer River · Dinosaur Park Formation · American Museum of Natural History

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Articulated skeletons, a series of skulls at successive growth stages, the internal airway of the crest, and scaly skin impressions.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: The crest is read as a species-specific display and resonating structure whose growth tracked maturity, and the many named Alberta lambeosaurines as a smaller number of species.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: The acoustic output of the living animal, any soft-tissue extension of the crest, colour, and the exact status of C. intermedius.
